items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A question worded so that it suggests a particular answer"?
options: Likert scale
questionnaire
non-response bias
leading question
items.answer: leading question
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of leading question.

items.stem: Freya writes: "A longer questionnaire always produces more valid data." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Long questionnaires cause fatigue and careless responding; validity depends on well-designed items that measure the construct, not length.
items.markingKey: Long questionnaires cause fatigue and careless responding; validity depends on well-designed items that measure the construct, not length. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between open questions and closed questions.
items.answer: Open questions let respondents answer freely, giving rich qualitative data that are hard to compare; closed questions offer fixed options, giving quantitative data that are easy to analyse but may force answers.
items.markingKey: Open questions let respondents answer freely, giving rich qualitative data that are hard to compare; closed questions offer fixed options, giving quantitative data that are easy to analyse but may force answers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to a school well-being survey, explain how it illustrates questionnaire design.
items.answer: A school in Singapore surveys 600 students using 20 Likert items on stress plus one open question: "What would most improve your well-being at school?" Likert items give comparable quantitative data on stress; the open question captures unexpected issues in students' own words
items.markingKey: Context (A school in Singapore surveys 600 students using 20 Likert items on stress plus one open question: "What would most improve your well-being at school?") – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Likert items give comparable quantitative data on stress; the open question captures unexpected issues in students' own words – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to questionnaire design.

items.stem:
Priya completed a questionnaire on attitudes to learning using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Items 1, 3, 5 are reverse-scored.
1. "I feel left out by my classmates." - response: 4
2. "I enjoy learning new things in school." - response: 5
3. "I give up easily on hard problems." - response: 1
4. "I feel I belong in my class." - response: 4
5. "I find it hard to stop scrolling at night." - response: 4

Calculate Priya's total score (higher = more positive attitude) and explain why some items are reverse-scored.
items.answer: Scored values: [2, 5, 5, 4, 2]; total = 18 (out of 25). Reverse-scored items reduce acquiescence bias and check that participants read each item.
items.markingKey: M1 reverse items 1, 3, 5 scored as 6 - response. A1 total = 2 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 18. R1 reverse-scoring controls acquiescence (yes-saying) and response sets.

items.stem: Write two Likert-scale items to measure attitudes to homework, one of which is reverse-scored, and explain how they would be scored.
items.answer: E.g. "Homework helps me understand lessons" (1 = strongly disagree ... 5 = strongly agree) and "Homework is a waste of my time" (reverse-scored: 5 becomes 1). Scores are summed so that higher totals mean a more positive attitude.
items.markingKey: E.g. "Homework helps me understand lessons" (1 = strongly disagree ... 5 = strongly agree) and "Homework is a waste of my time" (reverse-scored: 5 becomes 1). Scores are summed so that higher totals mean a more positive attitude.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Questionnaires are a valid way to measure attitudes."
items.answer: Questionnaires can measure attitudes validly if items are carefully designed, piloted and validated, but they should be triangulated with other measures.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: standardised, large samples, quick to analyse; validated scales (e.g. PSS) show good reliability. Arguments against: social desirability and acquiescence bias; self-report may not match behaviour; translation and cultural meaning of items. Supported judgement: Questionnaires can measure attitudes validly if items are carefully designed, piloted and validated, but they should be triangulated with other measures.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "pilot test"?
options: An item worded in the opposite direction, whose score is reversed before totalling, to reduce acquiescence bias
A graph that plots pairs of scores to show a possible correlation
A trial of the questionnaire on a small sample to identify unclear or problematic items before the main survey
Any systematic tendency to answer questions inaccurately or in a particular way
items.answer: A trial of the questionnaire on a small sample to identify unclear or problematic items before the main survey
items.markingKey: C. "pilot test" is a trial of the questionnaire on a small sample to identify unclear or problematic items before the main survey.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a questionnaire should be pilot tested.
items.answer: A pilot reveals ambiguous, leading or double-barrelled items, unsuitable response options, ceiling effects and timing problems, so the final questionnaire is more valid and reliable.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A pilot reveals ambiguous, leading or double-barrelled items, unsuitable response options, ceiling effects and timing problems, so the final questionnaire is more valid and reliable. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student's questionnaire includes the item "Do you use your phone in bed? Always / Sometimes" What is the main problem with this item?
options: ambiguous wording
double-barrelled open question
incomplete response options
double negative
items.answer: incomplete response options
items.markingKey: C. It is a incomplete response options: there is no option for "never" or "rarely".

items.stem: Nia recorded the following frequencies: System 1 answer = 22; System 2 answer = 48; no answer = 46. Calculate the percentage of the total that was "System 1 answer" (to 1 decimal place) and identify the modal category.
items.answer: 19.0%; modal category: System 2 answer
items.markingKey: A1 22/116 x 100 = 19.0%. A1 mode = System 2 answer (48).

items.answer: Problem: incomplete response options - there is no option for "never" or "rarely". Improved: "How often do you use your phone in bed? Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always".
items.markingKey: 1 mark: problem identified (incomplete response options). 1 mark: why it biases or confuses responses (there is no option for "never" or "rarely"). 1 mark: an improved item that removes the problem, e.g. "How often do you use your phone in bed? Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always".

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "acquiescence bias"?
options: The tendency to agree with statements regardless of their content ("yea-saying")
The tendency to answer in a way that will be viewed favourably by others
A graph that shows frequencies or means for separate categories, with gaps between bars
A graph that plots pairs of scores to show a possible correlation
items.answer: The tendency to agree with statements regardless of their content ("yea-saying")
items.markingKey: A. "acquiescence bias" is the tendency to agree with statements regardless of their content ("yea-saying").

items.stem: Briefly explain why social desirability bias is a problem in surveys.
items.answer: Respondents may over-report desirable behaviour (exercise, studying) and under-report undesirable behaviour (cheating, prejudice), so the data do not reflect reality and conclusions are invalid.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Respondents may over-report desirable behaviour (exercise, studying) and under-report undesirable behaviour (cheating, prejudice), so the data do not reflect reality and conclusions are invalid. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Online surveys remove all sampling bias because anyone can take part." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Online surveys exclude people without internet access and attract self-selected volunteers, which can create serious sampling bias.
items.markingKey: Online surveys exclude people without internet access and attract self-selected volunteers, which can create serious sampling bias. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe a survey on academic honesty and explain what it reveals about response bias in surveys.
items.answer: A school in Toronto asks students to report how often they cheat, using a paper questionnaire with their names on it, collected by their homeroom teacher. Named responses collected by a teacher create strong social desirability bias, so cheating is likely to be under-reported; anonymous online collection would help
items.markingKey: Context (A school in Toronto asks students to report how often they cheat, using a paper questionnaire with their names on it, collected by their homeroom teacher.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: named responses collected by a teacher create strong social desirability bias, so cheating is likely to be under-reported; anonymous online collection would help – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to response bias in surveys.

items.stem: A university team in Lima emailed an online questionnaire about screen use to 250 students; 100 completed it. Calculate the response rate and explain one way in which a low response rate could bias the findings.
items.answer: Response rate = 100/250 x 100 = 40.0%. Non-response bias: those who reply may differ systematically (e.g. more interested in or affected by screen use).
items.markingKey: A1 100/250 x 100 = 40.0%. R2 non-response (self-selection) bias explained in context: respondents may be more motivated or more affected by screen use, so results may not represent all 250 students.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Survey data are too affected by bias to be useful."
items.answer: Surveys are always vulnerable to bias, but careful design and sampling make them useful, especially when triangulated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: social desirability, acquiescence; non-response and volunteer bias. Arguments against: anonymity and careful design reduce bias; large samples give useful patterns; validated scales show good reliability and validity. Supported judgement: Surveys are always vulnerable to bias, but careful design and sampling make them useful, especially when triangulated.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "non-response bias".
items.answer: Bias that occurs when people who do not respond differ systematically from those who do
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: bias that occurs when people who do not respond differ systematically from those who do. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between non-response bias and volunteer bias.
items.answer: Non-response bias arises when invited people who do not respond differ from those who do; volunteer bias arises when people who choose to take part differ from the population.
items.markingKey: Non-response bias arises when invited people who do not respond differ from those who do; volunteer bias arises when people who choose to take part differ from the population. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Reverse-scored items help to detect acquiescence bias.
Reason (R): Acquiescence bias is the tendency to agree with statements regardless of content.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: B. Both true; R defines the bias but does not itself explain how reverse-scoring detects it (inconsistent agreement with opposite items).

items.stem: Lars recorded the following frequencies: integration = 28; assimilation = 37; separation = 45. Calculate the percentage of the total that was "separation" (to 1 decimal place) and identify the modal category.
items.answer: 40.9%; modal category: separation
items.markingKey: A1 45/110 x 100 = 40.9%. A1 mode = separation (45).

items.stem: A researcher in Hanoi wants a representative sample of 15-year-olds for a survey on sleep. Suggest a sampling method and two ways of reducing response bias.
items.answer: Stratified random sampling from school registers across districts and school types; anonymous responses, neutral wording, balanced and reverse-scored items, short questionnaire.
items.markingKey: Stratified random sampling from school registers across districts and school types; anonymous responses, neutral wording, balanced and reverse-scored items, short questionnaire.

items.stem: Define the term "Spearman's rho".
items.answer: A non-parametric correlation coefficient calculated from ranks, used with ordinal data or non-normal interval data
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a non-parametric correlation coefficient calculated from ranks, used with ordinal data or non-normal interval data. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Zara reports a correlation coefficient of -0.21 between years of experience as a taxi driver and posterior hippocampal volume rank. Interpret the direction and strength of this relationship, and suggest one third variable that could explain it.
items.answer: A weak negative correlation: as years of experience as a taxi driver increases, posterior hippocampal volume rank tends to decrease. Correlation does not establish causation; a third variable such as personality could affect both, or causality could run in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark direction (negative); 1 mark strength (weak, r = -0.21); 1 mark causality: no IV is manipulated, so third variables (e.g. personality) or bidirectional causality cannot be ruled out.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why percentages are often more useful than raw frequencies in survey results.
items.answer: Percentages allow comparison between groups of different sizes (e.g. 30 boys vs 70 girls) and show the proportion of respondents, which is easier to interpret. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Percentages allow comparison between groups of different sizes (e.g. 30 boys vs 70 girls) and show the proportion of respondents, which is easier to interpret. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to a survey on study habits, explain how it illustrates analysing survey data.
items.answer: A student survey in Accra finds that 62% of respondents study with music, and those who do report slightly lower concentration ratings. The percentage summarises a frequency; the comparison of ratings is correlational and self-reported, so causal conclusions about music are not justified
items.markingKey: Context (A student survey in Accra finds that 62% of respondents study with music, and those who do report slightly lower concentration ratings.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the percentage summarises a frequency; the comparison of ratings is correlational and self-reported, so causal conclusions about music are not justified – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to analysing survey data.

items.stem: Survey results: 48 students rated "I feel prepared for exams" as strongly disagree 6, disagree 10, neutral 14, agree 12, strongly agree 6. Identify the modal and median response and suggest an appropriate graph.
items.answer: Modal response: neutral (14). Median: the 24th and 25th responses are both "neutral" (cumulative 6, 16, 30), so median = neutral. Graph: bar chart of frequencies.
items.markingKey: Modal response: neutral (14). Median: the 24th and 25th responses are both "neutral" (cumulative 6, 16, 30), so median = neutral. Graph: bar chart of frequencies.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Descriptive statistics are sufficient for analysing survey data."
items.answer: Descriptive statistics are the starting point, but inferential tests and qualitative analysis are needed for full conclusions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: summarise large data sets clearly; percentages and modes suit categorical data. Arguments against: cannot show whether relationships are significant; correlation needs inferential testing; open responses need qualitative analysis. Supported judgement: Descriptive statistics are the starting point, but inferential tests and qualitative analysis are needed for full conclusions.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "scattergram"?
options: Bias that occurs when people who do not respond differ systematically from those who do
A table showing the number of responses in each category
A graph that shows frequencies or means for separate categories, with gaps between bars
A graph that plots pairs of scores to show a possible correlation
items.answer: A graph that plots pairs of scores to show a possible correlation
items.markingKey: D. "scattergram" is a graph that plots pairs of scores to show a possible correlation.

items.stem: A student claims: "If a survey shows a correlation of 0.6 between screen time and anxiety, screen time must cause anxiety." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Correlation shows association only; anxious people may use screens more, or a third variable may affect both.
items.markingKey: Correlation shows association only; anxious people may use screens more, or a third variable may affect both. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a bar chart and a scattergram.
items.answer: A bar chart shows frequencies or means for separate categories; a scattergram shows the relationship between two continuous variables measured for each participant.
items.markingKey: A bar chart shows frequencies or means for separate categories; a scattergram shows the relationship between two continuous variables measured for each participant. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A correlational study found r = 0.18 between years of experience as a taxi driver and posterior hippocampal volume rank. Describe this correlation and explain why it cannot be used to conclude that one variable causes the other.

"How many hours did you sleep last night? (0-4, 5-6, 7-8, 9+)"
"Tell me about your best holiday."
"What does friendship mean to you?"

questionnaire

Assertion (A): Online surveys always produce representative samples.

Choose the correct option.

items.markingKey: A1 25/91 x 100 = 27.5%. A1 mode = integration (46).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Survey data are too affected by bias to be useful."
items.answer: Surveys are always vulnerable to bias, but careful design and sampling make them useful, especially when triangulated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: social desirability, acquiescence; non-response and volunteer bias. Arguments against: anonymity and careful design reduce bias; large samples give useful patterns; validated scales show good reliability and validity. Supported judgement: Surveys are always vulnerable to bias, but careful design and sampling make them useful, especially when triangulated.

items.stem:
A researcher in Cape Town investigated the relationship between hours of revision and exam percentage in 7 participants.
Participant: hours of revision | exam percentage
P1: 36 | 26
P2: 21 | 28
P3: 19 | 32
P4: 26 | 19
P5: 24 | 22
P6: 23 | 14
P7: 28 | 17

Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs) using rs = 1 - 6Σd² / (n(n² - 1)), giving your answer to 3 decimal places. The critical value for n = 7 at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 0.786. State whether the correlation is significant and what can be concluded.
items.answer: Σd² = 80; rs = -0.429; moderate negative correlation; not significant at p = 0.05.
items.markingKey: M1 rank each variable separately (ranks X: [7, 2, 1, 5, 4, 3, 6]; ranks Y: [5, 6, 7, 3, 4, 1, 2]). M1 d² summed: Σd² = 80. A1 rs = 1 - 6(80)/(7(49 - 1)) = -0.429. A1 |rs| < 0.786, so the correlation is not significant; retain the null hypothesis. R1 correlation does not show causation - a third variable could explain the relationship.

items.stem: With reference to the six concepts of the course, discuss the claim that questionnaires are a valid way to measure attitudes.
items.answer: Questionnaires can measure attitudes validly if items are carefully designed, piloted and validated, but they should be triangulated with other measures.
items.markingKey: For: standardised, large samples, quick to analyse; validated scales (e.g. PSS) show good reliability. Against: social desirability and acquiescence bias; self-report may not match behaviour; translation and cultural meaning of items. Supported conclusion: Questionnaires can measure attitudes validly if items are carefully designed, piloted and validated, but they should be triangulated with other measures. Markbands (scaled to the marks available): top band - focused on the command term, accurate and detailed knowledge, research explicitly used as evidence, well-developed evaluation (methods, ethics, culture, alternative explanations) and a reasoned conclusion; middle band - mostly focused, relevant research partly linked, evaluation uneven; lower band - descriptive, research named but not used, little evaluation.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "pilot test".
items.answer: A trial of the questionnaire on a small sample to identify unclear or problematic items before the main survey
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a trial of the questionnaire on a small sample to identify unclear or problematic items before the main survey. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which strategy best reduces social desirability bias in a survey about drug use?
options: Using only open questions
Anonymous online responses
Face-to-face interviews with teachers
Asking students to write their names
items.answer: Anonymous online responses
items.markingKey: B. Anonymity reduces the pressure to present oneself favourably.

items.stem: Which measure of central tendency is usually most appropriate for responses to a single Likert item?
items.answer: The median or mode
items.markingKey: The median or mode. Single Likert items are ordinal.

items.stem: "A longer questionnaire always produces more valid data." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Long questionnaires cause fatigue and careless responding; validity depends on well-designed items that measure the construct, not length.
items.markingKey: Long questionnaires cause fatigue and careless responding; validity depends on well-designed items that measure the construct, not length. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between response bias and sampling bias.
items.answer: Response bias concerns inaccurate answers from the people who respond; sampling bias concerns who is included in the sample, making it unrepresentative of the population.
items.markingKey: Response bias concerns inaccurate answers from the people who respond; sampling bias concerns who is included in the sample, making it unrepresentative of the population. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a correlation between two survey variables cannot show causation.
items.answer: Neither variable is manipulated, so a third variable may explain both and the direction of influence is unknown; survey data are also self-reported.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Neither variable is manipulated, so a third variable may explain both and the direction of influence is unknown; survey data are also self-reported. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why reverse-scored items are included in a Likert questionnaire.
items.answer: They prevent respondents from agreeing with everything (acquiescence bias) and identify inattentive responding, because a consistent respondent must disagree with reverse-worded items.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They prevent respondents from agreeing with everything (acquiescence bias) and identify inattentive responding, because a consistent respondent must disagree with reverse-worded items. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a high response rate does not guarantee an unbiased sample.
items.answer: If the sampling frame itself is unrepresentative (e.g. only students in one school), or particular groups still fail to respond, the respondents may still differ from the target population.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If the sampling frame itself is unrepresentative (e.g. only students in one school), or particular groups still fail to respond, the respondents may still differ from the target population. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a scattergram and a bar chart.
items.answer: A bar chart shows frequencies or means for separate categories; a scattergram shows the relationship between two continuous variables measured for each participant.
items.markingKey: A bar chart shows frequencies or means for separate categories; a scattergram shows the relationship between two continuous variables measured for each participant. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Sofia completed a questionnaire on attitudes to learning using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Items 1, 2, 5 are reverse-scored.
1. "I often feel bored in lessons." - response: 3
2. "I give up easily on hard problems." - response: 1
3. "I enjoy learning new things in school." - response: 1
4. "I keep trying when work is difficult." - response: 1
5. "I feel left out by my classmates." - response: 3
6. "I feel I belong in my class." - response: 2

Calculate Sofia's total score (higher = more positive attitude) and explain why some items are reverse-scored.
items.answer: Scored values: [3, 5, 1, 1, 3, 2]; total = 15 (out of 30). Reverse-scored items reduce acquiescence bias and check that participants read each item.
items.markingKey: M1 reverse items 1, 2, 5 scored as 6 - response. A1 total = 3 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 2 = 15. R1 reverse-scoring controls acquiescence (yes-saying) and response sets.

items.stem: A university team in Lima emailed an online questionnaire about sleep habits to 800 students; 345 completed it. Calculate the response rate and explain one way in which a low response rate could bias the findings.
items.answer: Response rate = 345/800 x 100 = 43.1%. Non-response bias: those who reply may differ systematically (e.g. more interested in or affected by sleep habits).
items.markingKey: A1 345/800 x 100 = 43.1%. R2 non-response (self-selection) bias explained in context: respondents may be more motivated or more affected by sleep habits, so results may not represent all 800 students.

items.stem: Outline one way in which a survey on study habits shows analysing survey data.
items.answer: A student survey in Accra finds that 62% of respondents study with music, and those who do report slightly lower concentration ratings. The percentage summarises a frequency; the comparison of ratings is correlational and self-reported, so causal conclusions about music are not justified
items.markingKey: Context (A student survey in Accra finds that 62% of respondents study with music, and those who do report slightly lower concentration ratings.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the percentage summarises a frequency; the comparison of ratings is correlational and self-reported, so causal conclusions about music are not justified – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to analysing survey data.

items.stem: A questionnaire on student well-being in Singapore includes the item "Don't you agree that social media is harmful to teenagers?" Identify the problem with this item and rewrite it to improve it.
items.answer: Problem: leading question - it suggests the expected answer. Improved: "How, if at all, does social media affect you? (very negatively ... very positively)".
items.markingKey: 1 mark: problem identified (leading question). 1 mark: why it biases or confuses responses (it suggests the expected answer). 1 mark: an improved item that removes the problem, e.g. "How, if at all, does social media affect you? (very negatively ... very positively)".

items.stem: A researcher in Seoul emailed an online questionnaire about experiences of cyberbullying to 250 students; 53 completed it. Calculate the response rate and explain one way in which a low response rate could bias the findings.
items.answer: Response rate = 53/250 x 100 = 21.2%. Non-response bias: those who reply may differ systematically (e.g. more interested in or affected by experiences of cyberbullying).
items.markingKey: A1 53/250 x 100 = 21.2%. R2 non-response (self-selection) bias explained in context: respondents may be more motivated or more affected by experiences of cyberbullying, so results may not represent all 250 students.

items.stem: Outline one way in which a school well-being survey shows questionnaire design.

items.stem: "Descriptive statistics are sufficient for analysing survey data." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Descriptive statistics are the starting point, but inferential tests and qualitative analysis are needed for full conclusions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: summarise large data sets clearly; percentages and modes suit categorical data. Arguments against: cannot show whether relationships are significant; correlation needs inferential testing; open responses need qualitative analysis. Supported judgement: Descriptive statistics are the starting point, but inferential tests and qualitative analysis are needed for full conclusions.
